subtype: Sticking out the tongue in play and taste [Expressing]
passage:
“Ankita, look. Look at me.” Francis stuck out his tongue.
Ankita giggled and stuck hers out, crossing her eyes.
“Now it's a race,” said Francis. “Who can go furthest?”
Ankita shrieked and pushed her tongue out until she almost fell over.
Then he gave her a slice of lime. She licked it, screwed up her face, tongue poking out.
“Sour?” he asked.
“Yuck!” she said, and pushed the slice away.

qa.q: What did Francis give Ankita to lick?
qa.a: A slice of lime.

qa.q: What does Ankita's tongue mean in the lime moment, and what else could it mean?
qa.a: It probably shows mild disgust at the sour taste, since she said “Yuck” and pushed the slice away. Earlier, the tongue was just play.

qa.q: How could Francis respond next?
qa.a: He could laugh with her, put the lime away and go on with the tongue game, since a stuck-out tongue here is play, not rudeness.

qa.q: What might Ankita feel when Francis copies her?
qa.a: She may feel happy and clever that a grown-up joins in, which makes the game more fun.

grounding: A toddler sticks out her tongue in imitation play and in mild disgust at a sour taste, and the adult copies it playfully.

A buffalo ambled past the tea stall at the edge of the village, and Amandeep stuck his tongue right out at it. An old man at the next bench frowned. "Chhi, rude boy!"
Pradeep, Amandeep's chacha, just stuck his own tongue out at the buffalo too. Amandeep squealed and did it again, then again, looking back at Pradeep each time. "He's playing, uncle-ji," Pradeep said. "He's too little for rude."

qa.q: What walked past the tea stall?
qa.a: A buffalo.

qa.q: What did Amandeep's tongue out and squeal show he was feeling?
qa.a: He was being playful and silly, enjoying the game; checking back at Pradeep suggests he liked sharing it.

qa.q: Which reaction helped Amandeep more, and why?
qa.a: Pradeep's copying helped, because it matched his play and kept the moment warm instead of shaming him.

qa.q: How does the old man see the tongue?
qa.a: He sees it as rude, the way it would be from an older child, rather than a toddler's play.

grounding: A toddler sticks out his tongue in play, and his uncle copies it playfully instead of calling it rude.

In the kitchen of their Istanbul flat, Rafael squeezed a lemon over the salad. Elif reached for a slice. She licked it, and her tongue shot straight out. Her eyes squeezed shut and she shook her head.
Rafael laughed and stuck his tongue out back. "Sour!" Elif stared at him, then licked the lemon again, and out came the tongue once more.

qa.q: What was Rafael squeezing the lemon over?
qa.a: The salad.

qa.q: Why did Elif lick the lemon again after sticking her tongue out?
qa.a: She felt mild disgust at the sour taste, but her curiosity and Rafael's laughing made it into a funny game she wanted to repeat.

qa.q: What did Rafael do that suited Elif's age?
qa.a: He named the taste and copied her tongue playfully, rather than scolding or forcing her.

qa.q: How might Rafael feel watching Elif go back for more lemon?
qa.a: He likely feels amused and fond, enjoying her curiosity. 😄

grounding: A toddler sticks out her tongue at a sour taste, mild disgust that becomes play when her father copies it.

I'm Manoj. I keep the stationery shop near the school. On Tuesday a small boy, Chetan, sat on the counter while his grandfather bought pencils. He looked at me and stuck out his tongue. His grandfather went red. "Sorry, sorry, he has no manners!"
I wasn't sure if Chetan meant anything by it. So I stuck my tongue out too. Chetan's eyes lit up and he giggled, and did it again.

qa.q: What was Chetan's grandfather buying?
qa.a: Pencils.

qa.q: What might Chetan's tongue have meant?
qa.a: Most likely playfulness, a way to start a game with a new face; he may also just have been copying someone. His giggle shows he felt delighted when Manoj joined in.

qa.q: What would you tell Chetan's grandfather?
qa.a: That a toddler sticking out his tongue is usually play, not rudeness, and it is fine to join in.

qa.q: How does Chetan's grandfather feel about the tongue?
qa.a: He feels embarrassed and worried that it looks like bad manners.

grounding: A shopkeeper sees a toddler stick out his tongue and copies it playfully, unsure but guessing it is play.
